passage:
Friday
Dear Diary,
I planned my whole birthday today. Mushroom pizza, because it's the best food in the world, and then everyone watches the dinosaur film, because everyone loves dinosaurs. I told Ritu at recess and she made a face. She said she hates mushrooms and dinosaur films make her sleepy. I said, "No, you don't." She said, "Yes, I do, Zubin."
Then Arman said he likes paneer pizza better. And Chiku wants to play cricket in the park instead.
I felt weird and a bit angry. How can people not like mushrooms? Amma hugged me and said, "My boy, everybody's tongue is different." I still think they're wrong, but maybe I'll get two kinds of pizza.
- Zubin

qa.q: What did Chiku want to do instead?
qa.a: Play cricket in the park.

qa.q: Why was Zubin so surprised when Ritu made a face?
qa.a: He believed mushroom pizza and dinosaur films were loved by everyone, so it didn't make sense that a friend could feel differently. 😔

qa.q: What small step could Zubin take while planning the party?
qa.a: He could ask his friends what they like before deciding, and offer a choice, like the two kinds of pizza.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt when Zubin said, "No, you don't"?
qa.a: She might feel brushed aside, as if her own likes didn't count.

grounding: It shows a boy assuming his favourite food and film are everyone's favourites and feeling hurt when friends differ.

passage:
At the temple fair in Sirsa village, Ujjwal had saved twenty rupees for jalebis. "Everyone loves jalebi," he announced, buying a paper cone for himself and his friend Kishore. "And after this, gilli-danda behind the school. Everyone loves that too."
Kishore held the jalebi as if it might bite him. "It's too sweet for me. And I want to see the clay-doll stall. I don't really like gilli-danda."
Ujjwal stopped chewing. "How can you not like gilli-danda? The whole village plays it."
"Not everybody," Kishore said quietly. "You just always pick it."
Ujjwal's ears went hot. He'd thought they both loved the same things. He finished Kishore's jalebi too, and then, after a long moment, walked with him to the clay-doll stall.

qa.q: What did Kishore want to see at the fair?
qa.a: The clay-doll stall.

qa.q: What do Ujjwal's hot ears suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a little hurt, because he had believed Kishore loved the same things he did.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do next time he plans something with Kishore?
qa.a: Ask what Kishore would like, and take turns between gilli-danda and things Kishore enjoys.

qa.q: What has it been like for Kishore when Ujjwal always picked the game?
qa.a: Kishore went along quietly, perhaps without enjoying it, and only now said so.

grounding: It shows a boy assuming his friend loves the same sweet and game he does and being surprised when he doesn't.

passage:
"Okay, so on Friday we're all watching Robot Rangers Three," Javier told the lunch table at their school in Vancouver, "then we're playing tag in the gym, and my mom's making tamales. Everyone's favourite."
Chen poked at the rice. "I've never really liked Robot Rangers."
Javier stared. "But it's the best one. Everybody likes it."
"I like the nature ones. With the whales."
Maya added, "And I don't eat pork, remember?"
Javier's face fell. He'd pictured the whole evening, everyone cheering at the same parts. Now it felt like they were saying no to him, not to the film.
At home he told his mom, "Nobody likes my stuff."
She hugged him. "They like you. They just like different films."

qa.q: What is Javier's mom making on Friday?
qa.a: Tamales.

qa.q: Why does Javier feel as if his friends are saying no to him?
qa.a: He had pictured everyone loving the same things he loves, so their different tastes felt like rejecting him, not just the film.

qa.q: How could Javier plan Friday so more friends enjoy it?
qa.a: He could ask what they want to watch and eat, maybe letting everyone vote, or picking a nature film this time.

qa.q: How might Chen feel speaking up at the lunch table?
qa.a: Chen might feel a bit awkward disagreeing with Javier's excited plan, but wanted to be honest about liking nature films.

grounding: It shows a boy assuming his favourite film and food are everyone's and feeling hurt when friends differ.

passage:
The library period on Friday was for choosing the Class 4 film afternoon. Mrs D'Souza wrote three choices on the board: the space film, the animal film and the cartoon about a bus.
Vijay, nine, didn't even look. "Bus film. Everyone likes the bus film. And after, we can all have chilli chips, everyone's favourite."
The votes went up on the board. Bus film: 6. Animal film: 14. Space film: 11.
Vijay stared. "Preeti! You like the bus film. We watched it at my house."
"You liked it," Preeti said. "I fell asleep. And chilli chips make my mouth burn."
Vijay folded his arms and sat down hard. "Then why did you come to my house?"
"To play with your rabbit," Preeti said.

qa.q: How many votes did the animal film get?
qa.a: Animal film: 14.

qa.q: Why was Vijay so surprised by the vote?
qa.a: He was sure his own favourite film and snack were everyone's favourites, so seeing only six votes for the bus film felt shocking and even a bit like betrayal.

qa.q: What could Vijay try next time before announcing what everyone likes?
qa.a: He could ask his friends what they like first, and notice that Preeti might enjoy his house for the rabbit and not for the film.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel when Vijay asks why Preeti came to his house?
qa.a: Preeti may feel confused or a little hurt, since Preeti was just being honest and still likes visiting for the rabbit.

grounding: It shows a boy assuming all his friends love the same film and snack he does, and feeling surprised and hurt when they vote differently.

passage:
I'm Bhavna. My brother Kunal is eight, and on Sunday he planned the whole colony kids' afternoon without asking anyone.
He stood on the bench by the swings and announced: "First cricket, because everyone loves cricket. Then chocolate ice cream from the cart, because that's everyone's favourite. Then we watch the robot film at our house."
Ishita said she wanted to skip. Two boys wanted hide-and-seek. Someone asked for mango, not chocolate. Nobody had seen the robot film, and one girl said robots scared her.
Kunal went red. He kept saying, "But it's the best," louder each time. Then he climbed down and walked home alone.
I'm not sure if he was angry or just embarrassed. At dinner he asked me, quietly, what my favourite ice cream was. I said butterscotch. He looked really surprised.

qa.q: What did Kunal say they would do first?
qa.a: First cricket, because everyone loves cricket.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel when the other kids wanted different things, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kunal felt upset and embarrassed, going red and saying "But it's the best" louder each time before walking home alone.

qa.q: What small step by Kunal at dinner could help him next time?
qa.a: Asking Bhavna about her favourite ice cream was a good start; asking friends what they like before planning would stop him from being caught out.

qa.q: How might the other colony kids have felt when Kunal announced his plan?
qa.a: They may have felt ignored, since nobody was asked, and some, like the girl scared of robots, may have felt uneasy saying no.

grounding: It shows a boy assuming everyone shares his favourite game, food and film, and being surprised and hurt when they differ.

passage: Last month I had my birthday, and I planned everything myself. I'm Pankaj, and I love karela sabzi more than anything, so I asked Mummy to make a big pot for my friends. I also chose my favourite game, carrom, for the whole afternoon, and my favourite cartoon film for after. I thought everyone loves those things. When the plates came out, Usha made a face and pushed the karela to one side. Two boys wanted to play cricket instead of carrom, and nobody laughed at the film's jokes. My ears went hot and I went to the balcony. Usha came out and said, "Your party is nice. We just like different things." Next year I'm going to ask everyone first. But I'm still making karela.

qa.q: What food did Pankaj ask Mummy to make for the party?
qa.a: Pankaj asked for a big pot of karela sabzi.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj feel hurt when the friends didn't enjoy the party?
qa.a: Pankaj felt hurt and embarrassed, because karela, carrom and the film seemed like things everyone loves, so the friends' faces came as a shock.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try for next year's party?
qa.a: Ask each friend what they like to eat and play first, and maybe mix one of Pankaj's favourites with one of theirs.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt at the party?
qa.a: Usha probably didn't enjoy the karela but still cared about Pankaj, and so came out to the balcony to say the party was nice.

grounding: Shows a child assuming friends share the same favourite food, game and film, and feeling hurt when they differ.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Friday.
We voted today on where to go for the class trip. Before I even handed out the slips, Harsha stood up: "Everybody wants the planetarium! It's the best." Harsha said it the way you say the sky is blue. When I read the slips aloud, most said the zoo and a few said the water park. Only Harsha and Divyansh chose the planetarium. Harsha's face crumpled. "But why? Stars are the best thing." Divyansh leaned over and whispered, "I like stars too." I asked the class to each say one thing they liked about their choice. Harsha listened, arms folded, then said quietly, "Some people like animals more, I guess." I've promised Harsha and Divyansh a planetarium corner in the classroom next month.

qa.q: Which place got the most votes for the class trip?
qa.a: The zoo got the most votes.

qa.q: What does Harsha's crumpled face suggest about how Harsha felt?
qa.a: It suggests Harsha felt shocked and hurt, having been sure that everyone loved stars as much as Harsha does.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Harsha, and what else could help?
qa.a: The teacher had each child say what they liked about their choice, so Harsha heard real reasons; asking friends before announcing what everyone wants would also help.

qa.q: What was it like for Divyansh when the votes were read out?
qa.a: Divyansh was in the small group who chose the planetarium too, and whispered support, perhaps feeling a little left out as well.

grounding: Shows a child sure that everyone shares a favourite outing and being surprised and hurt by the class vote.

passage:
Sunday night
I made Sahil watch my favourite film today, the one with the robot dog. I've seen it eleven times. I was SO sure he'd love it, because everyone loves it, obviously. I even asked Ammi to make popcorn with extra butter, because that's how everybody likes it.
Sahil didn't laugh at the parts where I laugh. At the best bit, where the dog comes back, he was looking at his hands. After, he said, "It's okay. Bit babyish." BABYISH. My stomach dropped. Then he said his favourite is the scary ghost one, which I hate!! How can someone not like the robot dog?
Ammi said maybe next time Sahil picks the film. I said fine. But I am skipping the ghost parts.
Vaibhav

qa.q: How many times has Vaibhav seen the robot dog film?
qa.a: Vaibhav has seen it eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel so shocked when Sahil called the film babyish?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt hurt and stunned, because loving the robot dog film seemed like something everyone shares, so a friend not liking it felt impossible.

qa.q: What small step would help the next film night go better?
qa.a: Taking turns to choose, as Ammi suggested, or asking Sahil what films he likes before planning.

qa.q: What might Sahil have felt during the film?
qa.a: Sahil seemed bored and perhaps awkward, looking at his hands during the best bit and trying to be polite with 'It's okay'.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a friend loves the same film and snack, and feeling hurt on finding the friend's tastes differ.

passage: In the village of Wai, Santosh was planning his tenth birthday party. He was sure of everything. Everyone loved cricket, so they would play cricket all afternoon. Everyone loved gulab jamun, so Aai would make a hundred. When he told Ayesha from next door, she wrinkled her nose. "I hate cricket. Can we play kho-kho?" Santosh stared at her. "Everyone likes cricket." "I don't. And my brother doesn't like sweets." Santosh felt his face get hot. It felt like she was saying his party was bad. He went home and sulked on the step. Aai sat beside him. "Why don't you ask your friends what they'd like?" He didn't want to. But the next day he asked five friends. Three wanted cricket. Two wanted kho-kho.

qa.q: How many gulab jamuns did Santosh want Aai to make?
qa.a: A hundred.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when Ayesha said she hated cricket?
qa.a: He felt hurt and embarrassed, his face hot, because he had assumed everyone liked what he liked.

qa.q: What did Aai suggest, and what did Santosh find out?
qa.a: She suggested asking his friends what they'd like; three of five wanted cricket and two wanted kho-kho.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel about Santosh's plan?
qa.a: Ayesha might feel left out, since the party was planned around things she doesn't enjoy.

grounding: Shows a child assuming all his friends share his tastes in games, food and music, and feeling hurt when one disagrees.

passage: Lars was planning the film for his class's end-of-term party in Stockholm. It was obvious: the space-robot film he had watched eleven times. Everyone would love it. On Monday, Bilal, his best friend, said, "Oh no, not that one. I find it boring." Lars was shocked. "Boring? It's the best film ever. Everyone thinks so." "I don't. And the girls wanted the horse one." Lars felt a lump in his throat. How could Bilal not like it? At home he told his mother. She said, "You love it. That doesn't mean everyone does. Why not have a vote?" On Friday the class voted. The horse film won. The space-robot film came third. Lars was surprised, and a little hurt, but he sat next to Bilal anyway.

qa.q: How many times had Lars watched the space-robot film?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling when Bilal said the film was boring?
qa.a: He felt shocked and hurt, a lump in his throat, because he assumed everyone loved the film like he did.

qa.q: What did his mother suggest, and what did the vote show?
qa.a: She suggested a class vote, which showed the horse film won and his favourite came third.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel about disagreeing with his best friend?
qa.a: Bilal might feel a bit awkward, but honest, and glad Lars still sat next to him.

grounding: Shows a child sure the whole class loves his favourite film, and feeling hurt when his best friend and classmates choose differently.

passage: The Class 4 party at the Hyderabad school was on Friday, and Jahnavi ma'am asked Gautam to help plan the food. Gautam was delighted. He wrote on the board: "Menu: chicken biryani, chocolate cake, orange juice." Those were his favourites; surely they were everyone's. Jahnavi ma'am looked at the board. "Did you ask anyone?" "I don't need to. Everyone loves biryani." A girl in the second row put up her hand. "I don't eat chicken." Another said, "Orange juice makes my throat itch." Gautam's ears went red. He felt like they were attacking his menu. Jahnavi ma'am handed him a notebook. "Go round and ask each table what they'd like." He came back surprised. Six children were vegetarian. Four preferred lemon juice. Only the chocolate cake was a sure hit.

qa.q: How many children were vegetarian?
qa.a: Six children were vegetarian.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when classmates objected to his menu?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a bit attacked, ears red, because he assumed everyone shared his favourites.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi ma'am ask Gautam to do, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To ask each table what they'd like, so the menu reflected what classmates actually wanted, not just his own tastes.

qa.q: How might the girl who doesn't eat chicken have felt seeing the menu?
qa.a: She might have felt left out, since the main dish on the board was something she couldn't eat.

grounding: Shows a child planning a class menu from his own favourites, assuming everyone likes them, and being surprised when he asks.

passage:
Saturday, the first day of the winter holidays. Santosh planned his birthday party on a sheet of paper: gully cricket, chocolate cake, and the dinosaur film. "Everyone loves these," he told Amma. He didn't ask anyone.
Wednesday, the party. Noor sat out the cricket. Two boys asked for vanilla cake, which didn't exist. During the film, three kids drifted to the balcony to play carrom. Santosh's throat felt tight. "Why didn't anyone like my party?"
Friday. Noor came over with a leftover slice. "I liked the cake. I just hate cricket. You never asked."
Santosh thought about it. "What do you like?"
"Drawing. And carrom."
He wrote it down, surprised it was so different from his own list.

qa.q: What three things did Santosh plan for the party?
qa.a: Santosh planned gully cricket, chocolate cake and the dinosaur film.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when kids drifted to the balcony?
qa.a: Santosh felt hurt and confused, because he had been sure everyone liked what he liked.

qa.q: What could Santosh do before planning his next party?
qa.a: Santosh could ask friends what they enjoy, as he finally did with Noor, instead of assuming his favourites are everyone's.

qa.q: How did the party feel for Noor?
qa.a: Noor liked the cake but hated the cricket and felt unasked, which is why Noor came over to explain.

grounding: Shows a child who assumes all his friends like the same game, food and film he does and is hurt when they differ.

passage:
Jomon, you're sulking because your friends didn't want to play your game at Onam? Listen to your Seema Ammachi. Let me tell you about my brother Babu.
One Onam, when Babu was nine, he decided the sadya for his friends would be his. He loved bitter-gourd pachadi more than anything, so he told our Amma to make three times as much. "Everyone loves it," he said. He never asked.
At lunch, the friends ate the payasam, the banana chips, the avial, and left the pachadi in little green hills on every leaf. Babu's face went red. He ran behind the house and wouldn't come out.
Our grandmother found him there. "Babu, do you love every food?" He said no. "Then why should everyone love yours?"
Babu is fifty-three now. He still asks guests what they like before he cooks.

qa.q: What did Babu ask for three times as much of?
qa.a: Babu asked Amma to make three times as much bitter-gourd pachadi.

qa.q: What was Babu feeling when the friends left the pachadi?
qa.a: Babu felt hurt and embarrassed, because he had been sure everyone loved it as much as he did.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed Babu, and why?
qa.a: The grandmother's question, whether he loved every food, showed him his taste wasn't everyone's, and he began asking guests what they like.

qa.q: How might Babu's friends have felt at the sadya?
qa.a: They probably enjoyed the payasam and chips but felt a little awkward leaving the pachadi on every leaf.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a boy who assumed everyone loved his favourite dish and was hurt when friends left it.

passage:
On the last day before the summer holidays, Class 5 was allowed one film on the smart board, and Ma'am let Lokesh choose because he had the best attendance. There were only forty minutes before the buses.
Lokesh didn't even think. "The robot cartoon! Everyone loves it." He started it proudly.
Five minutes in, the ceiling fans stopped. Power cut. The smart board went dark.
In the sticky silence, Ma'am asked the class to vote on what to do instead.
"Antakshari!" someone shouted. "Story time!" "Nothing, let's just talk!"
"But the robot cartoon," Lokesh said. "Everyone wanted it."
Pradeep leaned over. "I've seen it nine times because of you. Half the class hates robots."
Lokesh stared at him, stung. He had never once wondered.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the buses?
qa.a: There were only forty minutes before the buses.

qa.q: Why was Lokesh so sure everyone wanted the robot cartoon?
qa.a: Lokesh felt confident and proud, assuming the film he loved was everyone's favourite, so he never checked.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do the next time he gets to choose for the class?
qa.a: Lokesh could ask for a quick vote, as Ma'am did after the power cut, before choosing.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel about the robot cartoon?
qa.a: Pradeep is tired of it after nine viewings and a little frustrated that Lokesh never asked.

grounding: Shows a child who assumes the whole class loves his favourite film and is stung to learn otherwise.

passage: Darshan's birthday fell in the Christmas holidays, and he planned the party in his Pune flat all by himself. Pani puri, extra spicy, because everyone loved pani puri. The racing video game, because everyone loved racing. And the dinosaur film, because obviously. When his friends arrived, Rekha took one puri and fanned her mouth. Two others asked if there was cake. Nobody wanted the racing game; they wanted carrom. When he put on the dinosaur film, Rekha said, "Again? We saw it in class." Darshan stood by the TV, holding the remote, his cheeks burning. "But everyone likes this," he said quietly. Rekha shrugged, not unkindly. "You like this."

qa.q: Which film did Darshan put on?
qa.a: The dinosaur film.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when Rekha said "Again?"
qa.a: He felt surprised and hurt, cheeks burning, because he had been sure everyone liked the same things he did.

qa.q: What could Darshan try when planning his next party?
qa.a: He could ask a few friends what they enjoy and offer a couple of choices of food and games, instead of guessing from his own favourites.

qa.q: How does Rekha see the party plan?
qa.a: Rekha sees it as Darshan's favourites rather than everyone's, which is why she says "You like this."

grounding: Shows a child assuming all his friends like the same food, game and film he does, and feeling hurt when they differ.
